questions.stem: A team declares `@interface RateLimit { int perMinute() default Limits.PER_MINUTE; }`, where `Limits` holds `static final int PER_MINUTE = Integer.getInteger("rate.perMinute", 60);`. What happens?

options.text: javac rejects the default, since PER_MINUTE gets its value only when the program runs
options.says: an element value must be a constant expression; a static final field initialised by a method call is not one

options.text: javac rejects the default, since PER_MINUTE is declared in a class other than RateLimit
options.says: a default may name another class's constant: Limits.MAX_ATTEMPTS, an int initialised with a literal, compiles

options.text: javac accepts it, and PER_MINUTE is read each time the annotation is read, since defaults are evaluated at run time
options.says: every element value, defaults included, is a constant fixed when javac runs

options.text: javac accepts it, and PER_MINUTE's value is stored as the default, since a static final int is a constant
options.says: a static final field is a constant only when its initialiser is itself a constant expression

origin.section: An Element Holds a Compile-Time Constant of a Few Types

questions.stem: The `catalog` service was compiled against release 1.4 of a library whose `@Cached` declares `int ttlSeconds() default 300;`. One method carries `@Cached`, another `@Cached(ttlSeconds = 60)`. Operations swap in release 1.5, where the declaration says `default 30`, and restart `catalog` without rebuilding it. Which TTLs does `catalog` read through reflection?

options.text: 300 and 60, since each method's class file holds every element's value as it was at compile time
options.says: a use site's class file records only the elements written there; the default is not copied into it

options.text: 30 and 60, since each method's class file holds only the elements written at that method
options.says: the default lives in the annotation type's class file and is filled in when the annotation is read

options.text: 30 and 30, since the new release's declaration replaces every value of that element
options.says: a value written at the use site is stored there and wins over any default

options.text: neither, since reading an annotation whose declaration changed after compilation throws
options.says: the page recompiled only the annotation type and the old class file read the new default without an error

origin.section: Defaults Live in the Annotation Type, and Only value Can Go Unnamed

questions.stem: A flags library declares `@interface Feature { String value(); boolean enabledByDefault(); }`, and a settings class writes `@Feature("dark-mode")` on a method. What happens?

options.text: It compiles, and enabledByDefault() returns false, since an omitted boolean element reads as false
options.says: an element without a default must be written at every use; there is no implicit false

options.text: It compiles, and enabledByDefault() throws when called, since that element was never given a value
options.says: javac refuses the use, so there is nothing to call

options.text: It doesn't compile, since enabledByDefault has no default and isn't written
options.says: value can go unnamed only when every other element has a default; javac reports the missing default for enabledByDefault

options.text: It doesn't compile, since the unnamed form needs a type with one element
options.says: @Endpoint("/orders") compiles with three other elements, because they all have defaults

origin.section: Defaults Live in the Annotation Type, and Only value Can Go Unnamed

questions.stem: `@Retention(RUNTIME) @interface Sensitive { }` is declared without `@Target`. A developer writes it on a field (`@Sensitive String token;`), on a method parameter, and inside a type argument (`Map<String, @Sensitive String> secrets;`). What does javac do?

options.text: It accepts all three, since a type with no @Target is allowed in every position
options.says: without @Target the annotation is allowed on declarations only, and refused in a type context such as a type argument

options.text: It accepts the field and the parameter and refuses the type argument, since without @Target only declarations qualify
options.says: an annotation type with no @Target applies to every declaration and to no type use; a type argument needs TYPE_USE

options.text: It accepts the field and refuses the parameter and the type argument, since without @Target only fields, methods and types qualify
options.says: with no @Target every kind of declaration qualifies, a type parameter and a method parameter included

options.text: It refuses all three, since a type with no @Target can't be written anywhere
options.says: @Tag without @Target compiled on a field and on a type parameter

origin.section: @Target Is Checked by javac at Every Use
